definition: Synthesize means to combine separate pieces into a new, coherent whole.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word synthesize. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know synthesize should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: For the capstone essay she had to synthesize forty years of court records and oral histories into a single argument.
Compile is weaker than synthesize: compiling gathers the pieces into one place and stops, while synthesizing works them into a new whole that none of the pieces contained alone.
Fuse goes further than synthesize — a synthesized whole still shows its working parts, but fused parts have melted together past the point of telling them apart.

Combine is the broad, everyday word for putting things together, in any way at all. Synthesize is more ambitious: the pieces are worked into a new whole — an argument, a compound — that none of them contained alone.
Integrate means fitting a part into a whole that already exists. Synthesize builds the whole itself, out of separate pieces that had never stood together before.

To synthesize is to combine separate pieces so that something new and whole comes out — an argument, a compound, a design.
The parts don't just sit side by side afterward; they are worked into a structure none of them contained alone.
academic / constructive — the researcher's verb
Synthesize is the researcher's verb, and rubrics love it because it asks for more than collecting.
Summarize shortens one source; compile gathers many; synthesize makes the many say something new together.
If nothing new stands at the end, the word hasn't been earned.

For years, the pieces of the Bitterroot fire mystery sat in separate buildings.
Satellite heat maps lived with the forest service.
Tree-ring cores sat in a university basement.
Retired crew chiefs kept their own logbooks at home.
Imani Okafor's insight was not a new measurement.
It was a decision to synthesize what already existed.
Her team spent two winters reading the three archives against each other, matching burn scars in the rings to dates in the logbooks and shapes on the maps.
The result was a fire-return model that none of the archives contained alone: a map of which valleys burn on a rhythm and which burn at random.
Reviewers noted that every fact in the model was already known to someone.
What was new was the whole.
